questions.q:
You are summarising the reasons why repair cafés have become popular. Text B includes these details:

A. The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009.
B. Visitors leave knowing how to sew on a button or replace a fuse themselves.
C. Manufacturers increasingly glue phones and laptops together.
D. Repairing a device saves the energy and raw materials needed to make a new one.

Identify the two details that are NOT relevant to the summary focus. [2]
ms: A — background/history, not a reason for popularity (1)
C — a problem/obstacle to repair, not a reason for popularity (1)
questions.tip: History and problems are the usual distractors in a summary text.

questions.q:
In a summary you should generalise lists and examples. Rewrite each of these as a short general phrase.
(a) “broken toasters, torn jackets and bicycles with flat tyres” [1]
(b) “how to sew on a button or replace a fuse” [1]
ms: (a) broken/damaged possessions / household items / belongings (1)
(b) basic/simple repair skills / how to fix things themselves (1)
questions.model:
(a) damaged household belongings
(b) basic repair skills
questions.tip: Ask: what do all the examples have in common? Use that as your phrase.

questions.q:
Rewrite this sentence from Text B in your own words, in no more than 15 words, keeping both ideas:

“Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish, and repairing a device saves the energy and raw materials needed to make a new one.” [3]
ms: Idea 1: helps reduce the rapidly increasing amount of discarded electronics / e-waste (1)
Idea 2: saves energy and resources/materials that would be used to manufacture replacements (1)
Own words (not ‘fastest-growing kinds of rubbish’, ‘raw materials needed to make’) and 15 words or fewer (1)
questions.model: Mending gadgets reduces soaring e-waste and conserves the resources used to manufacture replacements. (13 words)
questions.tip: Count your words — practising cutting sentences is the fastest way to stay under 120.

questions.q:
Text B – Fixing the throwaway habit (paragraphs 2 and 3)

The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009, and its appeal is easy to understand. Many modern goods are cheaper to replace than to repair in a shop, so people throw them away. At a repair café, a kettle that would have gone to landfill can be working again in twenty minutes, at no cost to its owner.
Visitors are not simply handed back their repaired items. They are encouraged to sit beside the volunteer and watch, and many leave knowing how to sew on a button or replace a fuse themselves. “It’s the knowledge that people value,” says one organiser. “Next time they won’t need us.”

Identify four reasons why repair cafés are popular from these paragraphs. Write them in note form, in your own words. [4]
ms: Repairs are free (1)
Cheaper than replacing items or paying a repair shop (1)
Repairs are quick (1)
Items are kept out of landfill / less waste (1)
Visitors learn practical skills by watching (1)
Visitors become independent — can fix things themselves in future (1)
questions.model:
• free of charge
• cheaper than buying new or using a repair shop
• fast
• visitors learn to do simple repairs themselves
questions.tip: Keep notes short — you’ll rewrite them as linked sentences in the final summary.

questions.q:
A student wrote this summary of the reasons why repair cafés have become popular:

“Repair cafés began in Amsterdam in 2009 and there are now more than two thousand. A kettle that would have gone to landfill can be working again in twenty minutes, at no cost to its owner. Many leave knowing how to sew on a button or replace a fuse themselves. There is tea and cake. I think every town should have one.”

Identify five weaknesses in this summary and suggest how to correct each one. [5]
ms: Irrelevant background (Amsterdam, 2009, number of cafés) — cut it (1)
Lifted/copied sentences — rewrite in own words (1)
Specific examples not generalised (kettle, button, fuse, tea and cake) — use general terms, e.g. ‘household items’, ‘basic repair skills’, ‘sociable’ (1)
Personal opinion at the end — remove; summaries are objective (1)
Important ideas missing, e.g. environmental benefits (saving energy/materials, e-waste) or volunteers’ sense of purpose — add them (1)
Disconnected, list-like sentences — link ideas with connectives (1)
questions.model:
1. The opening is background history, not a reason – cut it.
2. The second and third sentences are copied – rewrite them in my own words.
3. It uses examples (kettle, button, fuse, tea and cake) – generalise them, e.g. “household items are mended quickly and free”.
4. The last sentence is my opinion – delete it.
5. Key reasons are missing, such as saving energy and materials and giving retired volunteers a purpose – add them and link the ideas with connectives.
questions.tip: Before writing, check your plan against the four traps: background, examples, opinion, lifting.

questions.q:
Allow about 25 minutes.

Text B – Fixing the throwaway habit

On the first Saturday of every month, a church hall in Leeds fills with broken toasters, torn jackets and bicycles with flat tyres. This is a repair café, one of more than two thousand around the world, where volunteers mend people’s belongings for free.
The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009, and its appeal is easy to understand. Many modern goods are cheaper to replace than to repair in a shop, so people throw them away. At a repair café, a kettle that would have gone to landfill can be working again in twenty minutes, at no cost to its owner.
Visitors are not simply handed back their repaired items. They are encouraged to sit beside the volunteer and watch, and many leave knowing how to sew on a button or replace a fuse themselves. “It’s the knowledge that people value,” says one organiser. “Next time they won’t need us.”
For others, the attraction is environmental. Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish, and repairing a device saves the energy and raw materials needed to make a new one.
The cafés are also sociable places. There is tea and cake, and pensioners who once worked as electricians or tailors find that their skills are suddenly in demand again. Several volunteers say the cafés have given them a sense of purpose after retirement.
Some items, of course, cannot be saved. Manufacturers increasingly glue phones and laptops together, making them almost impossible to open, and some charge high prices for spare parts. Campaigners argue that new laws should give people a “right to repair”.

According to Text B, why have repair cafés become popular?
You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible.
Your summary should not be more than 120 words.
Up to 10 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 5 marks for the quality of your writing. [15]
ms: Indicative content:
1. Repairs are free
2. Cheaper than replacing goods / paying a repair shop
3. Repairs are quick
4. Items are kept out of landfill / less waste
5. Visitors learn basic repair skills by watching
6. Visitors can fix things themselves in future / become independent
7. Repairing saves energy and raw materials used to make new products
8. Helps tackle the fast-growing problem of electronic waste
9. They are friendly, social places (refreshments)
10. Retired people can use their old trade skills again / feel valued
11. Volunteering gives retired people a sense of purpose
Not relevant: Leeds church hall, Amsterdam 2009, number of cafés, glued phones/spare-part prices, right-to-repair campaign

levels.d: Thorough understanding; a wide range of relevant reasons (about 10–11), clearly focused on why the cafés are popular.
Good understanding; a range of relevant reasons (about 7–9); little irrelevance.
Some understanding; several relevant reasons (about 5–6), with some irrelevance or repetition.
Limited selection; may retell the text, include background/problems or copy extensively.
Concise, well organised, fluent and in own words throughout; within 120 words.
Mostly clear and in own words, with some lifting or wordiness.
Heavily copied, list-like or poorly organised; may exceed the limit or include opinion.

questions.model: Repair cafés have become popular because they mend broken possessions free of charge, which is far cheaper than buying replacements or paying a professional, and often very quickly. They stop usable items being thrown away, and repairing rather than replacing saves the energy and materials needed for new goods, helping to tackle the rapid growth of electronic waste. Visitors also learn basic repair skills by watching, so they can fix things themselves in future. The cafés are friendly social places, and retired people enjoy being valued again for their practical skills, which gives them a sense of purpose. (98 words)
questions.tip: Spend about 8 minutes planning, 12 writing and 5 checking the word count and lifted phrases.
